name: Educational Content
description: Educational content in Iran includes curriculum materials, broadcast lessons, digital textbooks, and resources for virtual classrooms. Institutional documentation shows particular attention to curriculum alignment and disability inclusion, while leaving important questions about implementation and learning outcomes unresolved.

seo.title: Educational Content in Iran: Digital Learning and Accessibility
seo.description: Explore Iran’s educational media, virtual learning policies, and accessible textbook initiatives, with distinctions between plans and verified delivery.

content.heading: Learning materials across different media
content.content:
Educational content is the material through which a lesson is communicated: an explanation, illustration, exercise, recording, or interactive activity. In Iran, the documented institutional landscape extends beyond electronic copies of books. UNESCO’s education technology profile identifies television, radio, and the Shad online channel among the tools used for distance education during the COVID-19 response. These are different delivery routes, rather than interchangeable measures of educational quality. A broadcast can distribute a lesson; a virtual classroom can also support exchanges between teachers and pupils. [s1]

For an international reader, the important distinction is between a learning resource and the system carrying it. Shad is a student education network, while a textbook, recorded explanation, or exercise is content. Describing a platform’s existence does not establish that every learner can obtain suitable material or use it successfully. The inspected policy profile documents intended functions, rather than an independent evaluation of their results. [s1]

content.heading: Curriculum alignment and teacher participation
content.content: UNESCO’s account of Iranian policy describes priorities for electronic textbook access and standards for producing educational resources. It also summarizes a 2022 Shad requirements document that calls for content production and editing, interactive virtual classes, and stronger digital literacy among teachers and students. These provisions connect content creation with classroom practice: distributing files is only part of the educational task. They are documented policy expectations, not proof of uniform implementation. [s1]

content.heading: Accessibility changes the content itself
content.content:
UNICEF Iran identifies inclusive digital learning platforms and digital textbooks among its education interventions, with attention to children with disabilities and refugee children. Its programme description places these resources alongside classroom expansion and support for pupils’ learning and retention. Digital publishing is therefore presented as one component of educational inclusion, rather than a substitute for schools and teachers. [s2]

A UNICEF consultancy document hosted by the United Nations in Iran gives a more concrete example. It describes HAMGAM, an accessible and inclusive digital learning platform being developed with the Special Education Organization. The document reports an interface and initial demonstration, while commissioning further development, testing, content adaptation, and deployment. It also describes earlier support for multimedia production facilities and teacher training. This establishes institutional activity, but does not establish completion of the commissioned platform. [s3]

The same document explains why accessibility requires editorial decisions as well as software. Narration, sign language, image descriptions, and interactive alternatives can convey information that a conventional page leaves inaccessible. Its proposed development process includes consultation with users and pilot testing. The practical implication is that a lesson must be reviewed in the forms learners will actually encounter, rather than judged only by its visual appearance. [s3]

content.heading: What the evidence can establish
content.content: These sources support an account of educational content as a combination of curriculum, production skills, distribution, and accessibility. They do not establish nationwide learning gains attributable to a particular platform. UNICEF’s programme statement expresses objectives, while the HAMGAM terms of reference distinguish an initial demonstration from work still being commissioned. Readers should preserve those differences when assessing claims about digital education in Iran. [s2][s3]

name: Advertising & Marketing
description: Advertising and marketing in Iran connect businesses with audiences through commercial messages, content, and distribution channels. Domestic advertising services operate within a wider environment shaped by platform restrictions, internet controls, and rules governing electronic commercial communication.

seo.title: Advertising and Marketing in Iran: Channels and Constraints
seo.description: Understand Iran’s advertising channels, domestic platforms, commercial communication rules, and the limits of available market evidence.

content.heading: A field spanning messages, media, and measurement
content.content:
Advertising purchases or arranges exposure for a commercial message. Marketing is the broader work of understanding an audience and connecting an offer with its needs. For this guide, the subject is divided into digital advertising, search engine marketing, social media marketing, content marketing, outdoor advertising, and advertising effectiveness. These branches overlap: a campaign may use an explanatory article, a paid placement, and a landing page while measuring their contribution together.

Iran’s domestic providers illustrate some of that overlap. Yektanet’s service catalogue includes website and application advertising, messaging, search-related services, and agency work. Tapsell lists web and in-application formats alongside placements associated with particular consumer services. Their catalogues establish what the companies advertise as available services; they do not independently establish market leadership or customer results. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Channels serve different purposes
content.content:
The distinction between a format and an objective is useful when reading Iranian advertising material. A banner is a presentation format; attracting recognition or generating an enquiry is an objective. Tapsell’s catalogue separates banners, video, native advertising, retargeting, and application-install services. That variety shows why the term digital advertising cannot be reduced to paid search alone. [s2]

Content marketing concerns useful or explanatory material intended to build a relationship with an audience. Search engine marketing concerns discovery through search, while social media marketing concerns communication within social platforms. Outdoor advertising places messages in physical settings. These distinctions organize the guide; they are not estimates of each branch’s share of Iranian expenditure. No verified national spending breakdown is presented here.

content.heading: Platform access shapes distribution
content.content:
International advertising infrastructure cannot be assumed to operate in Iran on the same terms as elsewhere. Google’s inspected policy lists Iran among the places where Google Ads is unavailable to advertisers and restricts location targeting. A domestic agency’s offer of Google-related services does not, by itself, establish that a particular advertiser or campaign is eligible under Google’s rules. [s3]

Iranian internet controls introduce a separate constraint. Freedom House’s 2024 assessment documents filtering, disruptions, and policies favouring domestic services during its reporting period. This is historical evidence of the operating environment, not a live list of blocked platforms in October 2026. The distinction matters because advertising depends on whether an audience can actually reach the publication, application, or destination carrying a message. [s4]

content.heading: Commercial messages and consumer information
content.content:
The Electronic Commerce Act text available through WIPO Lex includes provisions against misleading marketing, requires clear information about advertised goods and services, and calls for the beneficiary of an advertisement to be identifiable. These provisions show that electronic advertising is also a consumer information issue. They should not be read as a complete statement of all advertising rules or of present enforcement. [s5]

For readers, the useful question is whether a message makes its commercial purpose and responsible business understandable. A polished presentation does not establish the accuracy of the underlying offer. Equally, a legal provision establishes a stated obligation, rather than demonstrating that every advertiser complies with it. [s5]

content.heading: Reading performance claims carefully
content.content:
Provider websites combine service descriptions with promotional statements about reach and effectiveness. Those statements require different treatment. A listed format can establish that a provider markets that service; a claim of superior results requires evidence about the campaign, comparison, and measurement method. The inspected Yektanet and Tapsell pages do not supply an independent national benchmark for advertising effectiveness. [s1][s2]

A useful account of this field therefore keeps channel availability, commercial rules, and demonstrated outcomes separate. The sources establish a varied domestic service landscape and significant access constraints. A fuller picture still requires dated evidence on broadcast and outdoor advertising, regional markets, and comparable expenditure. Until those gaps are resolved, this page is an introduction to the field rather than a complete market assessment. [s1][s2][s3][s4]

name: Digital Advertising
description: Digital advertising in Iran includes paid placements on websites and inside applications, with domestic providers offering several formats and targeting services. Understanding the field requires separating an advertised service from verified campaign performance and distinguishing domestic internet restrictions from international platform policies.

seo.title: Digital Advertising in Iran: Formats, Networks and Access
seo.description: Learn how Iranian digital advertising services describe web and app placements, payment models, targeting, and international platform restrictions.

content.heading: Paid placements on websites and in applications
content.content:
Digital advertising places a commercial message within an online service. The advertiser supplies the offer, while a publisher provides space or access to an audience; an advertising platform may connect them. Iranian providers’ catalogues show both website and application placements. Yektanet also describes publisher monetization, illustrating the connection between advertisers seeking exposure and media owners seeking revenue. [s1]

Formats vary. Tapsell lists banner, video, native, push-notification, and application advertising services. Native advertising is presented in a form that resembles the surrounding publication, while a banner is a separate visual placement. These are format distinctions, not evidence that one produces better results in every setting. The provider’s catalogue is evidence of its marketed services, rather than an independent comparison. [s2]

content.heading: Payment models and targeting describe different things
content.content:
A format describes how an advertisement appears; a payment model describes what triggers a charge. Tapsell describes click advertising as a service in which the advertiser pays for clicks. Yektanet’s application advertising description names installation, click, and impression payment bases. Those events are different: displaying an advertisement, opening its destination, and installing an application are not interchangeable outcomes. [s1][s2]

Targeting is another layer. Yektanet describes selecting audiences using behaviour, location, and interests, alongside retargeting services. Such descriptions establish the company’s offer, but do not independently verify targeting accuracy or incremental sales. A report of campaign activity therefore needs a clear account of what was counted before it can support a claim of business success. [s1]

content.heading: International services have their own eligibility rules
content.content:
Google’s inspected policy states that Google Ads is unavailable to advertisers in Iran. It also says that physical presence in an embargoed region prevents account sign-in and that sanctioned countries cannot be selected for location targeting. These are Google’s stated product restrictions; they should not be generalized into a claim that every foreign digital service follows identical rules. [s3]

The policy also distinguishes specific location targeting from globally targeted campaigns. Consequently, seeing an advertisement while in Iran does not by itself establish that Iran was selected as its target. Likewise, an intermediary’s marketing offer cannot establish eligibility for every account or campaign. Provider descriptions and platform policy answer different questions. [s3]

content.heading: Access and accountability remain separate tests
content.content:
Domestic access conditions matter alongside international policies. Freedom House documented filtering and connectivity disruptions in its 2024 Iran report. Those findings explain a historical distribution risk, but do not establish which services were reachable everywhere at the later editorial cutoff. [s4]

Commercial accountability is a further issue. The Electronic Commerce Act text hosted by WIPO Lex addresses misleading advertising, clear product information, advertiser identity, and consumer choice over postal or email advertising. It also contains provisions concerning certain sensitive personal data. These are provisions in the inspected text, not a complete current compliance assessment. [s5]

Together, these distinctions make digital advertising easier to interpret: format, charging event, audience selection, access, and commercial responsibility each describe a different part of the activity. Evidence that a service exists should be kept separate from evidence that a campaign reached its intended audience or improved sales. [s1][s2][s3][s4][s5]
